title: Candour, raising concerns and escalation
blurb: Be open with women when things go wrong, know the statutory duty of candour, and raise and escalate concerns effectively.
question: On a day-3 postnatal visit, a community midwife finds that a woman's perineal tear involves the anal sphincter. It was recorded as second degree at birth, and she now needs repair in theatre. What should the midwife do about telling the woman?

teach.body: Candour means being open and honest with people when something goes wrong with their care. There are two duties. The professional duty (Code 14, and NMC and GMC joint guidance) applies to every midwife personally. The statutory duty (regulation 20 of the Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Regulated Activities) Regulations 2014) applies to registered providers in England, such as an NHS trust. SPM 1.19 links candour with courage, integrity and transparency.

teach.caption: Scotland (2016 Act) and Wales (2020 Act, from 1 April 2023) have their own organisational duties of candour.

steps.label: Apologise
steps.sub: To her and, if appropriate, family

steps.label: Escalate
steps.sub: Report so it is dealt with

teach.caption: Speak to the woman as soon as possible; you do not have to wait for an investigation.

teach.h: Reg 20: what counts as notifiable (health service body)
head: Harm
Meaning
rows: Moderate increase in treatment, e.g. unplanned return to theatre
teach.caption: Unintended or unexpected incident that could result in, or appears to have resulted in, one of these.

items: Notify the woman (the relevant person) as soon as reasonably practicable after becoming aware.
Do it in person: give a true account, say what further enquiries will happen, and apologise.
Follow up in writing with the same information and the results of any enquiries.
Keep a written record; if she cannot be contacted or declines, record the attempts.
An apology means 'an expression of sorrow or regret'. It is not an admission of negligence (Compensation Act 2006 s2).

teach.body: At Ewa's day-3 visit, midwife Kate finds a tear involving the anal sphincter, recorded at birth as second degree. Ewa needs repair in theatre: an unplanned return to surgery is moderate harm, so this is a notifiable safety incident for the trust. Kate's own duty is to arrange urgent review, explain honestly what she has found, say sorry personally, document it and report it through the incident system so the trust can complete the formal reg 20 process.

steps.label: Line manager
steps.sub: Verbally or in writing; keep a note

teach.caption: NMC recommends giving your name. Advice is available from Protect, unions and professional bodies. Code 16.5: never obstruct or victimise someone raising a concern.

teach.body: SPM 1.15 asks midwives to advocate, challenge colleagues and know when and how to escalate. If you believe a woman or baby is at risk (a worrying CTG, rising early warning scores, a plan you think unsafe), say so clearly, then escalate up the chain to the coordinator, senior obstetrician or consultant until the risk is addressed. Code 16.2: raise concerns immediately if asked to practise beyond your role.

teach.text: The statutory duty belongs to the ORGANISATION; the professional duty belongs to YOU. A midwife cannot wait for the trust's reg 20 letter before being honest with the woman. Also: an apology is not an admission of liability.

items: Code 14: put it right, explain fully and promptly, apologise, document and escalate.
Reg 20 (England): notifiable safety incident = death, severe, moderate or prolonged psychological harm (28+ days); notify in person as soon as reasonably practicable, apologise, then in writing.
Apology is an expression of sorrow or regret, not an admission of negligence.
Raise concerns: line manager, designated person, higher level, regulator; give your name; do not victimise others who raise concerns.
SPM 1.15: challenge colleagues and escalate until the risk to woman or baby is addressed.

summary: You can now apply the professional and statutory duties of candour to maternity incidents and explain what reg 20 requires of a trust. You can raise and escalate concerns through the right channels and challenge colleagues when women or babies are at risk.

A.q: A midwife realises she gave a woman a dose of an antibiotic intended for another woman. The woman is well. What should the midwife do first?
options: Complete an incident report before seeing her
Wait for the pharmacist's advice before telling her
Check the woman and act to put things right
Tell the woman at her next observation round
A.why: Code 14.1: act immediately to put right the situation where harm or potential for harm has occurred: assess the woman and get medical advice, then explain, apologise and report.

whyNot.0: Reporting is essential, but her safety comes first.
whyNot.1: She should be told as soon as possible; there is no need to wait for advice to be honest.
whyNot.3: Delaying until the next round is not prompt.

A.q: Who holds the statutory duty of candour under regulation 20 in England?
options: The individual midwife
The NMC
The CQC
The registered provider
A.why: Reg 20 places the statutory duty on registered providers (such as NHS trusts); the professional duty sits with each registrant.

whyNot.0: Midwives have the professional duty (Code 14); the statutory duty is the provider's.
whyNot.1: The NMC oversees the professional duty, not reg 20.
whyNot.2: The CQC regulates providers' compliance with reg 20; it does not hold the duty.

A.q: A woman asks whether the midwife's apology means the hospital admits it was negligent. What is the accurate answer?
options: Yes, an apology accepts legal fault for the trust
Yes, if the apology is given in writing
It depends on which professional apologised
No, an apology is not an admission of negligence
A.why: Compensation Act 2006 s2: an apology is not of itself an admission of negligence. Reg 20 defines apology as an expression of sorrow or regret.

whyNot.0: An apology does not of itself admit negligence.
whyNot.1: A written apology is required under reg 20, and is also not an admission of negligence.
whyNot.2: The legal position does not depend on who apologises.

B.q: After an incident, a woman develops anxiety and flashbacks that have lasted 6 weeks. Under reg 20, how is this harm classified?
options: Prolonged psychological harm
Low harm, not notifiable
Severe harm
No harm
B.why: Prolonged psychological harm is psychological harm experienced, or likely to be experienced, for at least 28 continuous days; 6 weeks meets this.

whyNot.1: Psychological harm lasting 28 days or more is notifiable.
whyNot.2: Severe harm means permanent lessening of bodily, sensory, motor, physiological or intellectual function.

B.q: A midwife raised concerns about unsafe staffing with her ward manager twice, with no change, and women are still waiting long periods for pain relief. What is the next appropriate step?
options: Post her concerns on a professional forum
Contact a newspaper with the details
Raise it with the designated person
Report the ward manager to the NMC
B.why: NMC guidance stages: line manager, then a designated person (such as a Freedom to Speak Up Guardian), then a higher level, then a regulator.

whyNot.0: Social media posting risks confidentiality and is not a proper channel.
whyNot.1: Going to the media is not an appropriate next step and may lose legal protection.
whyNot.3: The concern is about staffing, not the manager's fitness to practise.

B.q: A senior colleague tells a student midwife not to report a near miss 'because no harm was done'. What does the professional duty of candour guidance say?
options: Near misses need not be reported
The senior colleague decides on reporting
Report it under local policy
Report it if the woman asks
B.why: The NMC/GMC guidance covers reporting near misses through local systems, and says professionals must not prevent colleagues from reporting. Code 16.5 also forbids obstructing someone raising a concern.

whyNot.0: Near misses should be reported so lessons are learned.
whyNot.1: Seniority does not override the duty to report; colleagues must not be prevented.
whyNot.3: Reporting is not dependent on the woman's request.

C.q: A midwife is concerned that the CTG of a woman on oxytocin has become pathological. The registrar reviews it and says to continue. The midwife still believes the baby is at risk. What should she do?
options: Continue the oxytocin and record her view
Stop the oxytocin and escalate to the consultant
Ask another midwife to review it with fresh eyes
Wait for the next hourly CTG review
C.why: NG235 1.8.56: oxytocin must be discontinued immediately if the CTG is pathological, with urgent senior review. SPM 1.15 and Code 16.1: escalate concerns up the chain until the risk is addressed.

whyNot.0: Documenting doubts while continuing leaves the baby at risk.
whyNot.2: Fresh eyes are good practice, but with a pathological CTG on oxytocin she must stop it and escalate.
whyNot.3: Waiting delays action on a pathological trace.

C.q: At an incident meeting, the woman says she does not want to hear the details of what went wrong. What should the team do?
options: Give her the details in writing anyway
Respect her wish and record it
Tell her partner the details instead
Postpone until she agrees to listen
C.why: NMC/GMC candour guidance: if the person does not want details, respect this, record it, and tell them they can change their mind.

whyNot.0: Imposing details she has declined does not respect her wishes.
whyNot.2: Sharing with her partner without her agreement breaches her confidentiality.
whyNot.3: She should not be pressured; she can return to it when she chooses.

C.q: A midwife working in Cardiff discovers an incident that caused a woman more than minimal harm. Which statutory duty of candour applies to her NHS body?
options: Regulation 20 of the 2014 Regulations
The Health and Social Care (Quality and Engagement) (Wales) Act 2020
The Health (Tobacco, Nicotine etc. and Care) (Scotland) Act 2016
No statutory duty applies in Wales
C.why: The Welsh duty of candour (Health and Social Care (Quality and Engagement) (Wales) Act 2020 s3, in force 1 April 2023) applies to NHS bodies when a service user suffers unexpected or unintended harm that is more than minimal.

whyNot.0: Reg 20 applies to providers registered with the CQC in England.
whyNot.3: Wales has had a statutory duty of candour since 1 April 2023.

reteach.title: Mine and theirs
reteach.question: When something goes wrong, which candour duty is yours and which is the organisation's?

blocks.body: Your professional duty starts the moment you realise something has gone wrong: make it safe, tell the woman honestly, say sorry, write it down and report it. The organisation's statutory duty then takes over the formal steps: the in-person notification with a true account and apology, the written follow-up and the records.

blocks.text: A personal 'I am sorry' from the midwife is more meaningful than an organisational expression of regret, and it is not an admission of liability.

explain.body: 14.1 act immediately to put right; 14.2 explain fully and promptly and apologise; 14.3 document and escalate. Speak to the woman as soon as possible; do not wait for an investigation.

test.q: When should a midwife tell a woman that an error has occurred in her care?
options: After the investigation has concluded
Once the risk team has approved it
As soon as possible
At her postnatal discharge
test.why: NMC/GMC guidance: speak to the person as soon as possible; there is no need to wait for an investigation.

whyNot.0: Waiting for the investigation is not required and delays honesty.
whyNot.1: Approval from a risk team is not a condition of being candid.
whyNot.3: Waiting until discharge is not prompt.

explain.body: Provider duty in England. Notifiable safety incident: death, severe harm, moderate harm or prolonged psychological harm. Notify in person as soon as reasonably practicable, then in writing; keep records.

test.q: A baby needs an unplanned admission to the neonatal unit after an incident, and recovers fully within a week. Under reg 20, how is this harm best described?
options: Moderate harm
Severe harm
No harm
Low harm
test.why: Moderate harm includes a moderate increase in treatment such as transfer to another area like intensive care, with significant but not permanent harm.

whyNot.1: Severe harm is permanent; the baby recovered fully.
whyNot.2: The baby needed extra treatment, so harm occurred.
whyNot.3: Unplanned transfer to intensive care meets the moderate harm definition.

explain.body: Stages: line manager, designated person (e.g. FTSU Guardian), higher level, regulator. Give your name. Protect, unions and professional bodies can advise. Code 16.5: no obstruction or victimisation.

test.q: Why does the NMC recommend giving your name when raising a concern?
options: It makes investigation easier and gives best legal protection
It is required before a concern can be formally accepted
It means the concern is passed directly to the NMC
It allows the manager to decide whether action is needed
test.why: NMC guidance: giving your name makes the concern easier to investigate and gives the best legal protection, though confidential raising is possible within limits.

whyNot.1: Concerns can be raised confidentially; a name is recommended, not required.
whyNot.2: Giving your name does not change the route.
whyNot.3: Managers must act on concerns whether or not a name is given.

explain.body: SPM 1.15: advocacy and leadership, challenging colleagues and knowing when and how to escalate. Code 16.1: raise and, if necessary, escalate concerns about safety.

test.q: Which SPM proficiency asks midwives to challenge colleagues and know when and how to escalate concerns?
options: SPM 1.6
SPM 1.24
SPM 1.20
SPM 1.15
test.why: SPM 1.15: demonstrate the skills of advocacy and leadership, collaborating with and challenging colleagues as necessary, and knowing when and how to escalate concerns.

whyNot.0: SPM 1.6 is about being the accountable, autonomous lead professional.
